newsitem.title: USA: Dow soars to record close, bonds up, dollar weaker.
newsitem.headline: Dow soars to record close, bonds up, dollar weaker.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks soared to a record close for a second consecutive session Monday as the bull market kept up its stampede, sparked by hopes that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates unchanged.
Bonds edged higher and the dollar fell in listless trading.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 50.68, or 0.87 percent, at a record 5,889.20 after breaching the 5,900 level in late trading for the first time. On Friday, it set a new milestone of 5,838.52.
"It's pretty amazing. It's got 6,000 written all over it," said Jim Benning, a trader at BT Brokerage.
"It's more follow-through buying than anything else. Numbers are coming in perfect and there's the belief the Fed won't raise rates," he said.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 3.44 to 683.98, topping Friday's record closing high of 680.54.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks was up 1.72 to 365.42, surpassing its old record close of 363.74 set on May 24.
The Nasdaq Composite gained 5.29 to 1,193.96, still off the all-time high close of 1,249.15 set June 5.
In the broader market, advancing issues swamped declines 1,397 to 978 on heavy volume of 430 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Dow soared 178.66 points last week -- its second biggest weekly point gain ever as investors turned upbeat on economic data that pointed to moderating growth and benign inflation.
Last week, the government said the Consumer Price Index inched up just 0.1 percent and the Producer Price Index edged up 0.3 percent in August confirming that inflation was still dormant.
There had been widespread expectations that the Fed was ready to raise interest rates at the first sign of inflation.
Now, Wall Street is betting that the central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee will keep short-term interest rates unchanged at its next meeting on Sept. 24.

"It seems increasingly clear the Fed won't do anything," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter. "That means earnings are not at risk of a hike in interest rates and opens up a window of opportunity for stocks until the election," he said.
Some analysts were mystified by the stock boom, noting that fundmentals, such as moderating corporate earnings growth and a yield near 7 percent on the 30-year Treasury bond, remained worrisome.
In the bond market, the yield on the Treasury's 30-year bond held at Friday's close of 6.95 percent.
In late New York trading ,the dollar slid to 1.5110 German marks from 1.5134 marks late Friday and to 110.20 Japanese yen from 110.47 yen.
Grain prices fell sharply as weather forecasts pointed to better conditions for maturing corn and soybeans in the Midwest and oil prices fell on a rumour that Saudi Arabia would increase oil sales.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, December corn closed 7 cents a bushel lower at $3.14-1/2 and November soybeans closed 9 cents a bushel lower at $7.93.
December wheat futures closed at $4.17 a bushel, down 7 cents, after weekend news that Egypt, one of the biggest customers for U.S. wheat, bought 450,000 metric tons of wheat from France.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, October crude oil closed $1.32 lower at $23.19 a barrel. But October heating oil fell a sharp 2.65 cents a gallon to 65.29 cents and October unleaded gasoline closed 1.73 cents a gallon lower at 62.87 cents.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 ended 9.3 points higher at 3,977.2, beating Friday's close of 3,967.9. The Tokyo stock market was closed for a public holiday.
